title: When Man Asked: Who Created Me?
subtitle: A novel about the search for God, the beginning of creation, the truth of Islam, and the secret of life and death
genre: A contemplative literary novel with Islamic content
disclaimer: The novel's characters and dialogue events are fictional. The verses are taken from the Holy Qur’an, with the surahs and verses mentioned, and the transmitted hadiths are explained in their context. The literary text is not a fatwa or a specialized interpretation; It is recommended that it be forensically and editorially checked before official publication.

sections.title: In the footsteps of the prophets
Islam is in the details of life

pages.title: The night the question awoke
pages.content:
The city was not asleep, but Aser felt like the whole world had fallen silent. He sat near the window of his room, watching the rain draw curvy lines on the glass. A week ago, he had buried his father, and since that day everything familiar has seemed strange: the clock that does not stop, the street full of faces, and the sun that shines on those who laugh and those who cry without distinguishing between them.
He opened his phone and an old photo of his father appeared. He remembered the hand patting him on the shoulder when he was a child, and the question he would repeat without waiting for an answer: “Where do people go when they die?”
His father used to say: “To God we return.” But Aser was not sure that God existed at all.
He put on his coat and went out into the rain. He was not looking for a mosque or an argument, but rather a place where he could ask questions. At the end of the street, he noticed a small library whose light was still on, and on its door was a wooden plaque on which a single phrase was written: “Enter as you are, and ask as you wish.”

pages.title: Dar Al-Sual
pages.content:
Aser pushed the door open and heard the ringing of an old brass bell. Shelves of books stretched out in front of him, and the smell of paper and coffee crept into his chest. Behind the desk was a man over sixty, named Salim, with his glasses on top of an open book.
“You’re welcome,” Salim said with a smile. “The rain always brings us people who want to take shelter.”
Aser replied: “And I want to protect myself from an idea.”
The man raised his eyes. “Is the idea more dangerous than rain?”
“Sometimes,” Aser said after he sat down. I don't understand why we exist and then die. "I don't know why I'm supposed to believe in a God I haven't seen."
Salim did not get angry and did not rush to answer. He poured him a cup of tea, then said: “It's nice that you said what you're thinking clearly.” Faith is not sincere if we hide our questions.
At that moment a young woman entered carrying a book on religions. She identified herself as Maryam, and said she was a Christian who came to read about Islam. Shortly after that came Daniel, a young Jewish man who loved studying history. Thus began the story of four people who did not agree in belief, but agreed that the question deserved respect.

pages.title: Accept silence before answering
pages.content:
“Let's start from the beginning,” Aser said. Who created God?
He expected to see annoyance in Salim's face. But the man calmly leaned back and said: “The question is understandable, because we are accustomed to everything around us having a beginning.” But the Islamic faith does not say that God is one of the things of the universe until we search for a maker within the chain of things. It says that He is the Creator who is not preceded by nothingness, and whose existence does not depend on anyone else.”
Daniel said: “So we are not just talking about a being greater than the creatures, but about an existence different from them.”
Salim shook his head: “Yes. That is why the Qur’an says: ﴿لَيْسَ كَمِثْلِهِ شَيْءٌ﴾ [الشورى: 11]».
Aser was not immediately convinced. “This is a religious answer,” he said, “but why should I believe it?”
Salim replied: “I am not asking you to believe it because I said it. First understand what Islam claims, then test the arguments it presents, and read its texts. If we disagree, we will not spoil the truthfulness of the hadith.”
Outside, lightning struck the sky. And inside, Aser felt for the first time that his doubt would not be treated as a crime, but as a door that could be opened.

pages.title: Where did this existence come from?
pages.content:
Salim turned off the lamp near the window, and the sky became clearer. The stars appeared between the clouds like bright holes in an enormous curtain.
He said: “Look. We live in a world with laws, regularity and history. Science investigates how phenomena arise and develop, and this is great work. But the philosophical question of why there is something rather than nothing is another question.”
“We may not know the answer yet,” Aser said.
“This is a possibility that we should not be ashamed to acknowledge,” Salim replied. But the Qur’an invites you to contemplate the question of origin, not to close your eyes to it: ﴿أَمْ خُلِقُوا مِنْ غَيْرِ شَيْءٍ أَمْ هُمُ الْخَالِقُونَ﴾ [الطور: 35]».
He paused for a moment and then added: “This is not a physics equation, nor a substitute for scientific research.” “It is an invitation to think about what it means to exist at all.”
Maryam put her hand on the windowsill. “Sometimes we get so caught up in how things work that we forget to ask why they surprise us.”
As for Aser, he kept watching the sky. He did not find conclusive evidence at that moment, but he felt that the question had become broader than his personal grief.

pages.title: Is faith the enemy of reason?
pages.content:
“History is full of people who thought they were defending religion when they banned questions,” Daniel said as he turned the pages of his book. Does Islam want people to stop thinking?
Salim opened a small Qur’an and pointed to a verse: ﴿قُلِ انْظُرُوا مَاذَا فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ﴾ [يونس: 101].
He said: “This is an invitation to consider and contemplate. There are many questions in the Qur’an that address both the mind and the heart. But that does not mean that every unseen issue can be placed under a microscope or resolved with a laboratory experiment.
Aser smiled: “So you don’t want me to leave my mind outside the door?”
«بل أريدك أن تدخل به. And also allow him to know his limits. The great mind is not the one who claims to have all the answers, but the one who distinguishes between what he knows and what he does not know.”
There was a brief silence. Then Maryam said: “Blind faith may frighten people, and an arrogant mind may close other doors. “Maybe we need humility in both.”
“The search for God may begin when we stop being afraid to ask,” Aser wrote on a piece of paper in front of him.

pages.title: The noun that precedes nouns
pages.content:
The next morning Aser returned to the library. He found Salim writing a big word on a blackboard: “God.”
“Almost all religions talk about a god,” Aser said. What does this word mean in Islam?
Salim replied: “God in the Islamic conception is the One who has no partner, has no father or child, is not bound by an image that we can imagine, and is perfect in His knowledge, mercy, and justice. The Qur’an summarized this meaning in a short surah: ﴿قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ ۝ اللَّهُ الصَّمَدُ ۝ لَمْ يَلِدْ وَلَمْ يُولَدْ ۝ وَلَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ كُفُوًا أَحَدٌ﴾ [الإخلاص: 1–4].
“This is where important differences between Islam and Christianity emerge in understanding God and Christ,” Maryam said.
Salim replied: “It is true, and these differences are real and it is not right to erase them in the name of courtesy. But we can discuss it honestly and respectfully.”
Aser asked: “If God is perfect, why did He create us? Does he need us?
Salim replied: “According to Islam, God is in need of all the worlds.” We are the ones who need the meaning of our existence, not He who needs our worship.

pages.title: Why were we created?
pages.content:
The four went out to the library courtyard after the rain subsided. A drop of water was slowly rolling down a leaf, then falling onto the dirt.
“My question still stands,” Aser said. What is the purpose of a short life, filled with fear, loss, and fatigue?
Salim read: ﴿وَمَا خَلَقْتُ الْجِنَّ وَالْإِنْسَ إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُونِ﴾ [الذاريات: 56].
Aser frowned slightly: “Does this mean that life is all orders and rituals?”
Salim said: “Worship in Islam is broader than the form of prayer alone. It contains knowledge of God, love, and obedience to Him, and it contains the sincerity of the worker, the honesty of the doctor, the mercy of the father, and the fairness of the strong toward the weak. If a person intends it for the sake of God and adheres to goodness.”
Maryam added: “So the goal is not to remain inside a place of worship all day, but rather for life to have a moral and spiritual direction.”
He replied: “Exactly.” Islam does not deny the beauty of the world; Rather, he asks us how to live it without forgetting why we are here.”
Aser looked at another drop and asked himself: Could his life have a greater purpose than escaping pain?

pages.title: Where is God when we suffer?
pages.content:
This time the question did not come from Aser, but from Maryam. “I saw a child in pain in the hospital,” she said in a low voice. If God is merciful, why does He allow pain?
Salim was not in a hurry to answer. He said: “I do not know the wisdom behind every calamity, and it is not right for me to claim that I do. This question is one of the most profound matters discussed by believers and philosophers. Islam says that this world is not a place of final punishment, that man is tested, that God does not wrong anyone, and that the afterlife is a place where justice is achieved that we may not see here.”
He read quietly: ﴿الَّذِي خَلَقَ الْمَوْتَ وَالْحَيَاةَ لِيَبْلُوَكُمْ أَيُّكُمْ أَحْسَنُ عَمَلًا﴾ [الملك: 2].
Aser said: “But words do not take away the pain.”
Salim replied: “Correct. Therefore, it is not merciful to confront the suffering person with a lecture and then leave him alone. Faith that does not motivate us to console and help is deficient in its work.
Aser remembered his father's bed in his last days, and his sadness did not fade. But he found in the honest man's silence a respect for his pain that he did not find in many answers he had heard before.

pages.title: Between coincidence and meaning
pages.content:
Daniel took out a picture of a galaxy taken by a space telescope from his bag. He placed him on the table and said: “Whenever I see these pictures, I feel the smallness of man.”
“Maybe we are really small,” Aser said, “and the universe doesn’t have a message for us.”
Salim replied: “This is a possible explanation that some people adopt.” As for the believer, he reads the order and beauty of existence as two verses that call for contemplation of his Creator, without claiming that the image of a galaxy alone obligates everyone to believe.
Then he read: ﴿إِنَّ فِي خَلْقِ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضِ وَاخْتِلَافِ اللَّيْلِ وَالنَّهَارِ لَآيَاتٍ لِأُولِي الْأَلْبَابِ﴾ [آل عمران: 190].
Maryam smiled and said: “The verse does not describe the world as ugly so that we can escape from it to God. Rather, it invites us to see it well.”
Aser kept contemplating the picture: millions of distant lights, a small city, a small library, and a human being searching for enough reason to continue his life. He no longer saw his youth as an insult, but rather the beginning of humility.

pages.title: Chapter one
pages.content:
At the end of the week, Salim closed the Qur’an and placed it near a window overlooking the sea. He said: “We will not be able to establish the truth in sixty minutes. But we can give her sixty honest questions.”
Aser asked him: “Is it enough for me to feel astonished for me to believe?”
"no. Amazement is a beginning, not an end. Faith relates to evidence, reflection, spiritual experience and personal decision. We should not confuse the strength of our feelings with the validity of every conclusion we reach.”
Daniel said: “Let us move from asking about existence to asking about man. How does Islam narrate our beginning?
Salim got up and went to a shelf holding interpretation books, then returned them quietly. “We will read the Qur’an first, then distinguish what it explicitly mentions from what people narrate without a clear chain of transmission.”
Aser asked: “You mean Adam?”
“Yes,” said Salim. A story that does not begin with a perfect human being who does not make mistakes, but rather with an honorable creature who learns, chooses, becomes weak, and then knows the way back.
When they left the library, Aser realized that the question “Who created me?” It has become another question: “Who am I, and what is expected of me in this life?”

pages.title: Before the first human
pages.content:
The next night, there was a white paper on the table with a drawing of Salim in the middle of which was a small circle. He said: “Let us draw the beginning of the story as the Qur’an presents it, without adding details that it did not mention.”
Aser asked: “Does the Qur’an tell us how every atom, every galaxy, and every stage of Earth’s history came into being?”
"no. The Qur’an is a book of guidance, not an experimental encyclopedia. It states that God created the heavens and the earth, and calls for consideration of their creation, but it does not provide all the details that natural scientists investigate.”
Salim read: ﴿اللَّهُ خَالِقُ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ﴾ [الزمر: 62].
Daniel said: “People differ in interpreting some of the verses of creation, and linking them to modern discoveries may change as knowledge changes.”
Salim nodded in agreement: “For this reason, we should not interpret the verses as unbearable, nor should we claim that a scientific theory has been decided by a text that does not speak about it directly.”
Imagine Aser the land before the cities, before the roads, before the first house that opens its door to the morning. All human history seemed to him a small page in a vast cosmic book, and yet the Qur’an was going to make man the subject of a great moral question.

pages.title: Advertisement in the world of the unseen
pages.content:
He opened Salim Surah Al-Baqarah and said: “Here begins a strange scene from the story of Adam.” Then he read: ﴿إِنِّي جَاعِلٌ فِي الْأَرْضِ خَلِيفَةً﴾ [البقرة: 30].
Aser said: “Why did the angels mention that they fear corruption and bloodshed?”
Salim replied: “The verse mentions their question, and the divine answer comes: ﴿إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ مَا لَا تَعْلَمُونَ﴾. The story indicates that man is capable of doing good and evil, and that God’s knowledge is broader than the perspective of a creature.”
Maryam said: “So honoring a person does not mean that he is incapable of harm.”
"Yes. Rather, it means that he has a responsibility. The greatest dangers begin when the generous person thinks that he will not be held accountable.”
Aser looked at his hands. With the same hand he could pat a child on the head or hurt a person. With the same word, it can heal or break a heart.
The scene did not leave him thinking about the first humans alone; Rather, it prompted him to think about the person he creates every day with his decisions.

pages.title: Name and knowledge
pages.content:
Daniel said: “What is the first thing the Qur’an mentions about Adam’s peculiarity?”
Salim read: ﴿وَعَلَّمَ آدَمَ الْأَسْمَاءَ كُلَّهَا﴾ [البقرة: 31].
He said: “Expositors talk about the meaning of names and their teachings, and what concerns us here is that science is present at the heart of the story. “Adam is not presented as a mere body in motion, but as a creature who learns and receives knowledge.”
Aser smiled: “This is different from imagining that religion wants an ignorant person.”
“In the Qur’anic text, knowledge is not a defect. The shame is that it turns into arrogance, or that its owner uses it to despise others.”
Maryam opened a notebook and wrote: “The first blessing in the story is not strength, but the ability to understand.”
Aser remembered his father teaching him the name of the first star he saw from the roof of the house. The father did not know its scientific name, but he knew how to make the child look up. And Aser understood a little thing: knowledge begins with a name, but it does not end with it; It may turn into gratitude, or it may turn into pride, and the decision is up to its owner.

pages.title: The sin of pride
pages.content:
When they reached the story of Adam's prostration, Salim stopped for a long time at Satan. It read: ﴿أَبَى وَاسْتَكْبَرَ وَكَانَ مِنَ الْكَافِرِينَ﴾ [البقرة: 34].
Aser said: “Is the problem just a rejection of an order?”
Salim replied: “The scene highlights arrogance towards God’s command and contempt for others. In another place, Satan said: ﴿أَنَا خَيْرٌ مِنْهُ﴾ [الأعراف: 12].
Daniel said: “How many wars have started with those words without them being literally said? I'm better than him. Go higher. My relative purer. “My opinion alone is correct.”
Maryam lowered her gaze. “How many times has a religious person made a mistake by making his religiosity a reason for people’s contempt?”
Salim said: “When pride grows in the heart, its owner may carry a Bible but forget the first lesson in the story.”
Aser felt the words coming to him as well. He sometimes made fun of those who believed, and some of them made fun of his doubts. I realize that transcendence does not become a virtue if it wears the garb of reason, just as it does not become a virtue if it wears the garb of religiosity.

pages.title: Tree and selection
pages.content:
Aser asked: “What about the tree?” “Many people tell her story with details whose source I do not know.”
Salim said: “We are satisfied with what the Qur’an tells us. God placed Adam and his wife in Paradise, and forbade them from a tree, then Satan whispered to them, so they fell into what they were forbidden. The Qur’an does not specify the type of tree, nor does it make women solely responsible for the mistake.”
It read: ﴿فَأَزَلَّهُمَا الشَّيْطَانُ عَنْهَا﴾ [البقرة: 36].
Maryam said: “It struck me that they were mentioned together.”
“Yes,” Salim replied. In Al-A'raf we hear their joint confession: ﴿رَبَّنَا ظَلَمْنَا أَنْفُسَنَا﴾ [الأعراف: 23].
Daniel said: “Freedom, then, is not just a beautiful word; There is a possibility that we may choose wrongly.
Aser looked at his old notebook, remembering decisions he had made in anger and then regretted. He thought that the value of a person was to never fall, but the story leads him to a more difficult question: What does a person do after he falls?

pages.title: The first way back
pages.content:
Salim leaned over the Qur’an and turned its pages until the Almighty said: ﴿فَتَلَقَّى آدَمُ مِنْ رَبِّهِ كَلِمَاتٍ فَتَابَ عَلَيْهِ إِنَّهُ هُوَ التَّوَّابُ الرَّحِيمُ﴾ [البقرة: 37].
He said in a calm voice: “This is one of the most beautiful moments of the story.” "The mistake was made, but the door was not closed."
Aser asked: “Is a person born into Islam carrying the sin of Adam?”
“No,” Salim replied. One of the origins of the Islamic concept is that every human being is responsible for his work and does not bear the guilt of another person. God Almighty said: ﴿وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى﴾ [الأنعام: 164]».
“Here is an important theological difference from some Christian formulations of the question of original sin and salvation,” Maryam said.
“That's right,” said Salim. We understand the difference from the sources of each religion, and we do not attribute a single interpretation to everyone.”
Aser stopped at the word “and He repented to him.” He did not know whether he believed yet, but he found the meaning of pardon more merciful than his old conception of an endless court. Perhaps what he needed most was to believe that error is not a person's last name.

pages.title: Land is not a meaningless punishment
pages.content:
Aser said: “If Adam left Paradise for Earth, is the whole Earth just a punishment?”
Salim said: “The landing was linked to the violation that occurred, but the Qur’an mentioned before the story that Adam would be placed on earth. Human life here is not neglected: it contains guidance, assignment, trial, and work, as God says: ﴿فَإِمَّا يَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ مِنِّي هُدًى فَمَنْ تَبِعَ هُدَايَ فَلَا خَوْفٌ عَلَيْهِمْ وَلَا هُمْ يَحْزَنُونَ﴾ [البقرة: 38].
After talking, they went out into the street. The smell of bread comes from a small bakery, the sound of a child laughing from a nearby balcony, and a worker sweeping water off the sidewalk.
Maryam said: “If the earth were meaningless, the people on it would not need justice, mercy, and guidance.”
Daniel replied: “We would not have chosen so much weight.”
Aser stopped in front of the bakery and bought loaves for an old man sitting in the cold. This movement was not a solution to all his questions, but it revealed something to him: perhaps the meaning of life begins before the answer to every mystery in it is complete.

pages.title: Sons of Adam
pages.content:
On Friday, the library was crowded with new visitors. They included a migrant worker who spoke Arabic with difficulty, a female university student, and a man dressed in fancy clothes. Aser noticed that Salim served tea to everyone in the same way.
Daniel said: “What is the standard that elevates a person to God?”
Salim read: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَاكُمْ مِنْ ذَكَرٍ وَأُنْثَى وَجَعَلْنَاكُمْ شُعُوبًا وَقَبَائِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوا إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ أَتْقَاكُمْ﴾ [الحجرات: 13].
He said: “The verse addresses people, not one group. The criterion of dignity in the eyes of God is due to piety, not money, color, or lineage.”
“But people raise religious slogans and practice discrimination,” Aser said.
He answered: “Here we must differentiate between the principle that we read and the mistakes of those who claim to belong to it. Do not justify the mistakes of believers, and do not make them the only explanation for religion.”
Consider Aser the faces around the table. Each face had a history that it did not know, each one carried an unseen sadness, and they were all - according to the Qur’anic story - of one human origin.

pages.title: Is man free?
pages.content:
Aser said: “If God knows what we will do, are our choices real?”
Salim drew two lines on a sheet of paper, then stopped. “This is a profound issue in Islamic theology. Muslims believe in God’s knowledge and destiny, and in man’s responsibility for his voluntary actions, and scholars have differed in explaining the relationship between the two matters in many details.”
Daniel said: “It is not correct to present it as if it were a simple issue settled in one sentence.”
"correct. But it is clear that the Qur’an addresses man as responsible, and calls on him to make choices and be held accountable. This includes his saying: ﴿إِنَّا هَدَيْنَاهُ السَّبِيلَ إِمَّا شَاكِرًا وَإِمَّا كَفُورًا﴾ [الإنسان: 3].
Aser asked: “Is doubt a choice?”
Salim said: “Some of it may be an honest question, some of it is a deliberate stance, and I cannot judge a person’s intention by his appearance. The most important thing is not to deceive yourself: read what contradicts your opinion as well as what supports it.
Aser wrote: “Freedom is not just choosing what I want; Rather, I take responsibility for what I choose.”

pages.title: The first mirror
pages.content:
Before they turned off the lights, Salim placed a small mirror on the table. He asked Aser to look at her and then asked him: “What do you see?”
“A tired face,” he said, “and some early gray hair.”
Salim said: “And I see a human being capable of asking, loving, oppressing, apologizing, building, and destroying. “This frightening and beautiful ability is part of our responsibility.”
He lifted the Qur’an and read: ﴿وَلَقَدْ كَرَّمْنَا بَنِي آدَمَ﴾ [الإسراء: 70].
Maryam said: “An honor that cannot be nullified by differences in religion, lack of money, or the body’s inability to move.”
Daniel added: “And if we are honorable, we should not treat others as objects.”
Aser looked at the reflection of his eyes, then gently put down the mirror. He and his friends have reached the end of the first chapter of the human story. He did not suddenly become a man who knew everything, but he became wary of the word “mere”: just a body, just a number, just a passing person.
Salim said as he closed the door: “Tomorrow we will hear the story of those who came after Adam; Men and women who walked among the people and brought what they said was a revelation from God.”

pages.title: When people forgot the way
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
An old map of the world hung in the library. Daniel stood and traced the rivers and mountains with his pinky finger, then said: “Human beings dispersed across the earth, and their languages ​​and beliefs differed. How does Islam view their journey?
Salim said: “The Qur’an narrates that God sent messengers to people for guidance, and that the call to monotheism was the origin of their message. God Almighty said: ﴿وَلَقَدْ بَعَثْنَا فِي كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ رَسُولًا أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ وَاجْتَنِبُوا الطَّاغُوتَ﴾ [النحل: 36]».
Aser asked: “Does this mean that every prophet brought a religion that was identical in every detail?”
“No,” said Salim. The common origin in the Islamic conception is the monotheism and worship of God, with some laws differing according to nations and times.”
Maryam said: “Do we know the names of all the prophets?”
"no. The Qur’an mentions some of them, and says that there are messengers whose news God did not relate.”
Consider the Aser map; The borders drawn on it no longer represent only a history of wars, but a history of people asking the same question in different languages: How do we live on earth without getting lost?

pages.title: Noah's ark
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
The wind was so strong that evening that the library window began to shudder. Salim closed the wooden shutter, and said: “This is a sound that reminds me of the story of Noah.”
He read from Surat Nuh: ﴿إِنِّي دَعَوْتُ قَوْمِي لَيْلًا وَنَهَارًا﴾ [نوح: 5].
He said: “The Qur’an depicts a prophet making a long call to his people, facing denial, and then comes God’s command to build the ship. “There is patience and accountability in the story, and it is not just an image of a large ship in a rough sea.”
Aser asked: “What about those who did not believe him?”
Salim said: “The Qur’anic text narrates what happened to them, and it is religious news about God’s justice and judgment. But we should avoid inventing numbers and details that are not proven in the text.”
Daniel said: “The story of the Flood also appears in the Jewish and Christian heritage, although the narratives and interpretations differ.”
At that moment they heard a child crying in the street. Aser came out carrying his umbrella to help his mother cross the pooling water. When he returned, he said: “Perhaps being patient with people is more difficult than being patient with the storm.” Salim smiled: “That is why the stories of the prophets remain close to us.”

pages.title: A man looked at the stars
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
Daniel turned off the light on his phone and sat near the window. “I want to know Abraham,” he said. We find him in all our traditions, yet we differ in many details of his story.”
He opened Salim Surah Al-An’am at the verses that narrate Abraham’s looking at the planet, the moon, and the sun, then he said: “Abraham appears in the Qur’an searching for the truth, protesting against the worship of what is coming and going, turning to the Creator of the heavens and the earth.”
It read: ﴿إِنِّي وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِيَ لِلَّذِي فَطَرَ السَّمَاوَاتِ وَالْأَرْضَ حَنِيفًا﴾ [الأنعام: 79].
Aser said: “The question about the sky was long centuries before us.”
“And he is still there,” Salim replied. But Abraham in Islam is not just a thinker, but rather a prophet who received revelation, was tested, and obeyed.
Maryam said: “Perhaps what touches me most in his story is his courage in going against what his people were accustomed to.”
Aser asked: How often do you hold on to an idea because everyone around him is repeating it? How many times has he rejected another idea because it came from someone he disagreed with? He felt that intellectual courage might be difficult both ways.

pages.title: Meaning of delivery
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
Salim took out an old copy of the Qur’an, and opened it to the story of Abraham and his son when the great test came. It read: ﴿فَلَمَّا أَسْلَمَا وَتَلَّهُ لِلْجَبِينِ﴾ [الصافات: 103].
“This is an intense scene,” Aser said. How do Muslims understand it?
Salim replied: “As an exceptional trial by divine revelation to Abraham, it ended in redemption, and it is not permission for any human being to harm his child in the name of a vision or a religious claim. Judgments are not extracted from a story taken out of its context.”
Daniel said: “The religious narratives differ in some details related to the story.”
Salim nodded: “We respect the existence of real differences, and we explain what the Qur’an says without mocking others.”
Then he added: “Islam, in the origin of the word, relates to submission to God. But surrender is not a license to disrupt the mind nor to follow anyone who claims to speak in the name of God.
Aser was silent. He knew people who used the name of religion to impose their whims. He realized that it was important to always ask: Is this a fixed command from God, or a human desire trying to put on the garment of holiness?

pages.title: Joseph and the old shirt
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
An elderly woman came to the library asking about Surah Yusuf. She was carrying a shirt of a child she lost years ago, and was searching for words to help her be patient.
Salim chose to read some Surah with her, then he told his companions after her departure: “Joseph, son of Jacob, peace be upon them both; His story begins with envy of brothers, and passes through oppression, separation, strife, and imprisonment, then comes moments of empowerment and forgiveness.”
Maryam said: “It is a story in the middle of which the reader thinks that evil has won.”
Salim replied: «That is why it carries the meaning of patience without denying pain. At the end of the meeting, Joseph says to his brothers: ﴿لَا تَثْرِيبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْيَوْمَ﴾ [يوسف: 92].
Aser said: “Forgiveness here does not mean that what they did was good, but rather that Joseph chose not to imprison his future within what they did.”
The shirt remained fresh in his mind. He could not bring back the absent, but he realized that oracle stories do not always present a life without misfortune; Rather, it presents pictures of how to live after calamity, and gives the heart a chance not to turn to stone.

pages.title: Moses at the sea
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
Daniel asked: “Let us stop with Musa. Not just a name in a book; “For me, it is the heart of an entire religious history.”
Salim said: “The Qur’an glorifies Moses, peace be upon him, and mentions his standing in the face of Pharaoh, the oppression his people faced, and how the revelation came with guidance.”
It read: ﴿إِنَّنِي أَنَا اللَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا أَنَا فَاعْبُدْنِي وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِذِكْرِي﴾ [طه: 14].
Maryam said: “I like the image of the prophet who does not seek power for himself, but rather stands before an authority that deifies itself.”
Daniel added: “But we must allow each religious tradition to explain Moses from its sources as well. Similarity does not cancel out difference.”
Salim said: “Agreed.”
Aser asked: “What can a person today take from the story, even before he is convinced of the revelation?”
Daniel said: “At least injustice does not become a right with the number of its soldiers.” Salim continued: “And in faith, the greatest authority on earth is not a god, no matter how arrogant you are.”

pages.title: Mercy Maryam
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
One cold evening Maryam put the little cross she was carrying on the table, and said: “I don't want it to be the subject of a harsh argument. But I want to know how the Qur’an talks about Maryam the mother of Christ.”
“With love and reverence,” Salim said gently. An entire surah was named after her, and the Qur’an mentions her selection, purity, and the fear and loneliness she faced at the birth of Jesus, peace be upon him.
It read: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ اصْطَفَاكِ وَطَهَّرَكِ وَاصْطَفَاكِ عَلَىٰ نِسَاءِ الْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [آل عمران: 42].
Maryam's eyes filled with tears. “I did not expect to hear her name in this position in an Islamic text.”
Salim said: “The Qur’an mentions the birth of Jesus without a father as one of the signs of God’s power. Islam does not detract from Christ or his mother when it disagrees with the Christian conception of his nature.”
Aser said: “Can we differ in belief without making the difference an insult?”
“We should be able to,” Maryam replied. Otherwise it will not be a dialogue, but a battle of words.”

pages.title: Who is Jesus in Islam?
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
They returned to the question that Maryam left open. “I believe in Christ in a different way than you do,” she said. What exactly does Islam say about him?
Salim replied: “Muslims believe that Jesus, son of Maryam, is the Messiah, a noble messenger of those who have power. He was born by a miracle, and God supported him with miracles and revealed the Gospel to him. But in the Islamic faith, he is the servant of God and His Messenger, and he is neither a god nor a son of God.
Read the saying of Jesus in the Qur’an: ﴿إِنِّي عَبْدُ اللَّهِ آتَانِيَ الْكِتَابَ وَجَعَلَنِي نَبِيًّا﴾ [مريم: 30].
Maryam said after thinking: “So the disagreement between us is not only about the name of Christ or His love, but rather about the nature of Christ and the meaning of salvation, crucifixion, and resurrection.”
“Yes,” said Salim. The Qur’an presents a different perspective on basic issues, including what relates to killing and crucifixion, as in the case of women: 157. It would not be dishonest to claim that the three religions agree on everything.”
“And yet we still sit at the same table,” Aser said.
Maryam smiled: “Because my dignity does not depend on you agreeing with me, and your dignity does not depend on me agreeing with you.”

pages.title: The book that preceded the book
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
Daniel took out a translated copy of the Torah and placed it next to the Qur’an. He said: “Does Islam reject everything that preceded the Qur’an?”
“No,” said Salim. One of the foundations of the Islamic faith is the belief that God revealed books to His messengers, including the Torah and the Gospel, and that the Qur’an came to confirm and dominate the truth that God revealed. At the same time, the Islamic perception does not automatically equate all texts and interpretations existing today with the original revelation.
It read: ﴿وَأَنْزَلْنَا إِلَيْكَ الْكِتَابَ بِالْحَقِّ مُصَدِّقًا لِمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ وَمُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ﴾ [المائدة: 48].
Daniel said: “I now understand the place of the Qur’an in your faith, even if I do not share it.”
Salim replied: “This is a valuable understanding in itself. The goal of dialogue is not to attribute to others what they do not believe in.”
Consider Aser the two books. How many people spend their lives reading, interpreting and praying? He felt that religious history could not be summed up in a sarcastic sentence or a passing clip on a phone.

pages.title: The last promise
pages.section: In the footsteps of the prophets
pages.content:
At the end of the library was a painting of ancient Arabia, caravan routes, sand, and small towns. Salim said: “After the stories of the prophets, we come to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, whom Muslims believe is the final prophet.”
Aser said: “Why did God send prophets, instead of appearing to people and everyone immediately believing?”
Salim replied: “This is a philosophical question about the nature of faith and affliction. The Qur’an states that the messengers are human beings who convey God’s revelation, who call and explain, and who do not have the power to force hearts to believe.
It read: ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ [الأنبياء: 107].
Maryam said: “I want to know the biography from its beginning, not from the conflicting images that I receive.”
Daniel said: “And I want to distinguish historical facts from popular narratives.”
Salim closed his notebook. “We will start from Mecca, from a person who lived among his people before the revelation, and they knew his honesty and honesty. Then we follow the call as preserved by Islamic sources, while acknowledging the points of historical research when necessary.
When they left, Aser had a new question: How did one man in an ancient trading city become the author of a letter that people would read centuries later?

pages.title: City before dawn
pages.content:
Salim was describing Mecca, so it appeared to Aser narrow roads between the mountains, caravans entering the markets, and houses around the Kaaba. He said: “Muhammad bin Abdullah, peace and blessings be upon him, was born in Mecca in the sixth century AD. He grew up as an orphan and then lost his mother at a young age. His society had strong tribal ties, and aspects of chivalry and generosity, as well as injustices and customs that Islam denounced.
Maryam asked: “Did he seek power before he said he was a prophet?”
Salim said: “Biography books describe him as being known among his people for honesty, and he worked in trade, then the revelation came to him when he was forty.”
Aser said: “Many people sum up the life of the person they disagree with to the worst story they have ever heard about him.”
Salim replied: “That is why we read the biography from its sources, and differentiate between true and weak information and historical interpretation.”
Imagine Aser a man crossing the Mecca market. The passers-by do not know that his name will be mentioned in a call to prayer uttered in cities that did not exist at that time. The beginnings were often quieter than we imagine when looking at them from the end of history.

pages.title: Read
pages.content:
Salim closed the curtains of the library, then lit a small lamp over the Qur’an. He said: “In the Cave of Hira, according to the famous Islamic narration, the revelation began to descend upon the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him, through Gabriel, peace be upon him.”
He read slowly: ﴿اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ ۝ خَلَقَ الْإِنْسَانَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ ۝ اقْرَأْ وَرَبُّكَ الْأَكْرَمُ﴾ [العلق: 1–3].
Aser said: “The first word: Read. “It is strange that the message begins with an act related to knowledge.”
Salim said: “Knowledge should be associated with the name of the Creator. But let us not forget that the revelation was a solemn event, as authentic hadiths narrate; The Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him, returned to Khadija, may God be pleased with her, with his heart trembling, so she comforted him and reminded him of his noble qualities.
Maryam said: “At this moment there is a strong presence of a wife supporting her husband, not a marginal figure.”
He pictured in his imagination Aser a simple house, a man frightened by what he saw, and a woman saying words of confidence to him. The start of the humanitarian mission seemed closer to him than he expected.

pages.title: The first to believe
pages.content:
Salim said: “When we read the biography, it is not right to forget Khadija, may God be pleased with her. She was the first of the people to believe in the message of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, and she stood by his side in the difficult beginnings.”
Daniel asked: “Could it be that the great message began in a home, before it reached the squares and markets?”
He replied: “This is what the biography tells us.” This has a beautiful meaning: security and trust in the closest relationships may be a support for carrying the most severe responsibilities.
Aser said: “Where was his call headed?”
Salim said: “To unite God, abandon the worship of idols, establish justice, and reform the heart and behavior. This brought him and his first followers opposition and harm.”
“Real change doesn’t always start with applause,” Maryam said. Sometimes it begins with a person standing alone in the face of what people are accustomed to.”
Aser looked at preserved letters from his father, which contained short encouragements that he had written to him during his school days. I realize how one phrase in an hour of fear can carry its owner for a long time. He wrote in his notebook: “Behind much courage is a hand not mentioned in the headlines.”

pages.title: When the weak became visible
pages.content:
Aser asked: “What made the call of Islam influential in people’s lives, not just in their beliefs?”
Salim said: “It called for the worship of God alone, and linked faith to justice, mercy, and caring for the needy. The Qur’an condemns those who expel the orphan and does not encourage feeding the poor, as in Surah Al-Ma’un.
It read: ﴿أَرَأَيْتَ الَّذِي يُكَذِّبُ بِالدِّينِ ۝ فَذَٰلِكَ الَّذِي يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ﴾ [الماعون: 1–2].
Maryam said: “There is no meaning to worship that takes its person to a holy place, and then leaves it to despise a poor person.”
Salim replied: “This is one of the meanings determined by the texts. But Muslims, like other human beings, may do well or fall short. We must be held accountable for actions fairly.”
Daniel asked: “And rights in historical reality?” It must be studied in its complexity, not in a naive, idealistic way.”
“Sure,” said Salim. Differentiating between the standard that religion calls for, and the history of the societies that bear its name, prevents blind glorification and unjust generalizations.”

pages.title: Migration: the courage to leave
pages.content:
In the morning the sea was calm, so they went out walking along it. Salim said: “In Islamic history, the migration from Mecca to Medina came after years of preaching and persecution, and it was the beginning of a new phase in building society.”
Aser said: “Is leaving sometimes more courage than defeat?”
"Yes. Constancy is not always measured by staying in the same place. Preserving oneself, religion, and the ability to work may be a legitimate reason for moving.”
Daniel said: “What about those who couldn’t leave?”
He answered: “We must not erase the different human circumstances when we read history. Duties, abilities and necessities are not equal.
Aser stood looking at a bird flying off the beach. He had been clinging to his room since his father's death, until the place itself began to weigh on him. It occurred to him that he could change some details of his day without betraying the memory.
“Maybe we don't always need a new city,” Maryam said. “Maybe sometimes we need to break away from a habit that corrupts our hearts.”
Salim smiled: “This is a beautiful contemplative meaning, even if the historical migration is a real event with its own circumstances.”

pages.title: What is the Qur’an?
pages.content:
They returned to the library, and Aser put his hand on the Qur’an and asked: “Are these the words of the Prophet Muhammad, or the words of God, as Muslims believe?”
Salim said: “The Muslim believes that the Qur’an is the word of God that was revealed to Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, in the Arabic language, and that the Prophet conveyed it to the people. It is neither a biography of the Prophet nor a chronological book of events; It contains doctrine, legislation, stories, sermons, and an invitation to contemplation.”
Maryam said: “What is the difference between reading the Arabic text and translating it?”
He answered: “Translations convey the meanings of the Qur’an to the extent of the translator’s understanding, but the Qur’anic text that Muslims worship and recite is Arabic. Therefore, it is important in dialogues not to rely on one translation without awareness of its limitations.”
Aser asked: “How do I read it without cutting a verse so that it appears to contradict others?”
He said: “Read the context, refer to the reliable interpretation, pay attention to the reasons for the revelation and the language, and do not attribute an idea to the Qur’an just because a single sentence resembles it.”
He opened Aser Al-Fatihah for the first time with the intention of understanding, not with the intention of searching for an error to win an argument.

pages.title: Question of rhetoric and evidence
pages.content:
Aser said: “Muslims see the Qur’an as a miracle. But how does a non-Muslim examine this claim?
Salim replied: “He gets to know the text in its language as much as possible, and studies the history of its transmission, its content, its impact, and the miraculous aspects presented by Muslim scholars. Can seriously discuss evidence and objections; He is not asked to judge before reading.
Then he read: ﴿أَفَلَا يَتَدَبَّرُونَ الْقُرْآنَ﴾ [النساء: 82].
Daniel said: “Contemplation does not mean that we see in every verse what we want to see in advance.”
“Sure,” said Salim. It is not right to make hasty scientific claims on the text, then change its interpretation whenever theories change.”
Maryam said: “Honesty in research may make a person acknowledge that a question has not yet been decided.”
Aser felt strangely at ease. He was no longer required to claim certainty in a single day. Reading this time was like opening a window in a room that had been closed for years, and not declaring victory over someone sitting across from him.

pages.title: A messenger lives among the people
pages.content:
Aser said: “I want to know Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, in his daily life, not just in the big headlines.”
Salim said: “The hadiths narrate that he encouraged gentleness, mercy, and good treatment. And from his saying: “He who does not have mercy will not be shown mercy” [Agreed upon].”
Maryam said: “It is easy for a person to remember mercy, but it is more difficult to adhere to it when he is angry or in power.”
Salim replied: “That is why the example remains a test for those who follow it. It is not enough to love the Messenger with our tongue if we wrong people with our actions.”
Daniel asked: “Is it right to limit ourselves to pleasant narratives and neglect difficult historical questions?”
“No,” said Salim. A faithful study of the biography includes the facts, contexts, discussion of the chains of transmission and explanations, and does not evade the question. But it also does not base a judgment on an unknown narration or a passage without context.”
Imagine Aser the Messenger as a human being who eats, walks, grieves, and rejoices, and in the Islamic conception he receives revelation and conveys it. The distance between the majestic name and the human life that its owner lived has diminished.

pages.title: There is no compulsion in the heart
pages.content:
Maryam said: “I fear religious dialogue when it turns into pressure.” “Does our sitting here have to end with us converting to Islam for Salim to consider it a successful dialogue?”
Salim looked at her for a long time and then replied: “I do not own your heart, and I have no right to reduce our friendship to a result imposed by anyone. I am a Muslim. I believe that Islam is true, and I would like people to understand it, but one of the principles of its call is God’s saying: ﴿لَا إِكْرَاهَ فِي الدِّينِ﴾ [البقرة: 256].”
Daniel said: “There are also jurisprudential and historical discussions about the relationship of religious communities to difference, which are more complex than quoting a single verse.”
“That is true,” said Salim. But the meaning of the verse regarding the origin of entering into faith prevents us from making belief the result of fear.”
“So can I keep asking?” Aser said.
“That's why this table exists,” Salim smiled.
The three felt that the library door became wider. Each of them had the right to research, object, and be convinced or not, and respect remained despite the difference in the path.

pages.title: Islam, faith and charity
pages.content:
Salim pulled out a book of hadith and said: “There is a great hadith known as the hadith of Gabriel, narrated by Muslim, that explains the levels of religion.”
Then he explained: “Islam is manifested in the Shahada, prayer, zakat, fasting, and Hajj for those who are able. Faith includes belief in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, the Last Day, and destiny, its good and its evil. Ihsan is to worship God as if you see Him, and if you do not see Him, He sees you.”
Aser said: “So Islam is not just a word of social affiliation?”
He said: “Rather, it is belief, work and heart. A person may perform some manifestations and not achieve their full effect on himself, and for this reason a person always needs to review.”
Maryam said: “The word charity attracts me; "It's as if she's asking what we do when no one sees us."
“Yes,” Salim replied. Surveillance is not an abstract terror, but an awareness that God is aware of what is secret and what is revealed, and that sincerity changes the value of work.”
Aser wrote at the top of a new page: “If religion is a path, where does the first step begin?” He knew that the following conversation would delve into the details of life itself.

pages.title: The word changes direction
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
Aser said while turning the cup of coffee in his hands: “What does a person who is convinced of Islam and wants to enter into it say?”
Salim replied: “He bears witness that there is no god but God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, and he is aware of their meaning and believes in them. The first is the monotheism of God in worship, and the second is belief in the message of Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, and following him.”
Aser said: “Is speech sufficient for someone who does not believe in his heart?”
Salim said: “Faith is not an empty vocal performance. Testimony is a statement of belief, not a magic word. Whoever converts to Islam begins a journey of learning and work, not a journey of claiming that he has become infallible.”
“I would love for you to explain this without looking at me as if you were waiting for a decision,” Maryam said.
He smiled: “Every person is responsible for his own research, and I cannot choose instead.”
Aser began repeating the phrase to himself without saying it. It was surprisingly short, but it conveyed a complete conception of the universe, revelation, and life. Realize that great sentences are not those that are easy to say, but rather those that are understood to change the way you live.

pages.title: Five minutes before eternity
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
In the middle of the conversation, the Maghrib call to prayer rose from a nearby mosque. Salim stopped, then said: “I will pray and come back.” He asked Aser to accompany him without participating in the prayer.
He stood at the edge of the mosque, watching rows of people who did not know each other shoulder to shoulder. A rich man is next to a worker, and a young man is next to an old man, and they are all standing in one direction.
When Salim returned, Aser asked him: “Why do you repeat the prayer every day?”
He said: “Because people forget.” Prayer is a connection with God, a remembrance of Him, and a renewal of the covenant. The Qur’an says: ﴿وَأَقِمِ الصَّلَاةَ لِذِكْرِي﴾ [طه: 14]».
Aser said: “Does prayer automatically make a good person?”
He answered: “Performance is not a substitute for sincerity of heart and good work. The Qur’an states that prayer forbids indecency and evil [Al-Ankabut: 45], so if its effect is not reflected in our behavior, then we must review ourselves.”
Aser stopped at the door of the mosque. He had not made a decision of faith, but he understood why people returned to this pose five times a day: not because the world was quiet for them, but because they needed a steady point in the midst of its noise.

pages.title: Money does not remain yours alone
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
On Saturday morning, he found Aser Salim counting donations to buy school bags for children in need. He said: “Is this zakat?”
He replied: “It may be voluntary charity.” As for zakat, it is an obligation with specific conditions, shares, and disbursements, which make the money a duty towards those who deserve it.
It read: ﴿خُذْ مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِمْ صَدَقَةً تُطَهِّرُهُمْ وَتُزَكِّيهِمْ بِهَا﴾ [التوبة: 103].
“The idea of ​​social responsibility also exists in other religious traditions, but its details differ,” Daniel said.
Salim said: “This is something that should be considered fairly. In Islam, the goal is not to impoverish the owner, but rather to purify his relationship with money and help the deserving person in accordance with the provisions of zakat.
Aser looked at the small blue bag, and imagined a child proudly carrying it to school. He said: “Is giving still good if people know the name of the donor?”
“It may be overt or covert, but intent matters,” Salim said. In the authentic hadith: “Actions are but by intentions” [Agreed upon].
Aser put the bag back in the box and he understood that the value of something is not measured by its price alone, but rather by what it unlocks in the life of another person.

pages.title: Hunger teaches the heart
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
Ramadan was approaching, and small lanterns were hung in the market. Maryam asked: “What does it mean for a person to avoid food and drink for long hours?”
Salim said: “Fasting in Islam is an act of worship from dawn to sunset in Ramadan, in which the fasting person abstains from things that break the fast with the intention of worship. The purpose is not limited to feeling hungry; “It is about piety and self-control.”
He read: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ الصِّيَامُ كَمَا كُتِبَ عَلَى الَّذِينَ مِنْ قَبْلِكُمْ لَعَلَّكُمْ تَتَّقُونَ﴾ [البقرة: 183].
“But some people fast and then get angry and hurt others,” Aser said.
Salim replied: “This is why fasting also educates people, and its desired effect is not achieved by hunger alone. Sharia law takes into account cases of illness, travel, and other excuses stated in its provisions.”
Maryam said: “It is nice for the will to learn how to say no, even when you can say yes.”
Aser looked at the crowded market. He thought that freedom meant satisfying every desire, then he thought: Maybe it is freedom to own ourselves when desires multiply.

pages.title: A trip to the old house
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
On the library screen appeared a picture of the Kaaba surrounded by crowds of pilgrims. Daniel approached and said: “I know that Hajj has a connection with Abraham in Islam. But what does today mean?
Salim said: “Hajj is an act of worship performed in Mecca at a specific time, once in a lifetime if one is able, and it has well-known rituals. It is linked to the remembrance of God and the story of Abraham and his family, and it reminds the Muslim of his unity with believers who came from all over the earth.
Aser said: “It strikes me that people leave the usual decorative clothes and wear similar clothing during ihram.”
He replied: “This is a reminder of humility, even though the details of Ihram and its provisions remain broader than this symbolic meaning.”
Maryam said: “Is travel enough for a person to become good?”
Salim smiled: “Worship is not a tourist trip that guarantees change once the plane arrives. Its value lies in its correct performance and the piety and work it leaves behind.”
Aser looked at the faces in the picture. Imagine their different languages, their stories, and the hopes and sorrows they carry, then imagine them meeting in one prayer. The scene seemed like a practical answer to a question that has always bothered him: What can bring people together who differ in almost everything?

pages.title: Does morality require religion?
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
Aser sat up straight and said, “I know people who do not believe in God and are honest and merciful. I know religious people who lie and hurt. Why do I need religion to be a moral human being?
Salim said: “It is not right to deny the goodness that exists in a non-believer, nor to claim that every religious person has good morals. The deeper question concerns the source and purpose of moral standards, and how belief in God and accountability connect them. This is an issue that philosophers are seriously discussing.”
It read: ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُ بِالْعَدْلِ وَالْإِحْسَانِ﴾ [النحل: 90].
Maryam said: “If a religion calls for justice, its followers should not escape criticism when they are wronged.”
Daniel said: “The mind, conscience, and human experience are elements that people discuss, no matter how different their beliefs are.”
“Yes,” Salim replied. Islam does not teach a person to despise those who do good to him because he disagrees with him, but rather commands him to be just and righteous.
Aser felt that the answer did not try to cancel his experience. That was important; Honest talk does not require distorting the beautiful side of the other in order to defend himself.

pages.title: The mother who does not wait for thanks
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
Salim's phone rang. His elderly mother was asking for her medicine. Leave the conversation for a while and contact someone who can deliver what she needs. Then he came back apologizing.
Aser said: “Does Islam give the family a special status?”
“Yes,” said Salim. The Qur’an links the worship of God with kindness to parents, and mentions the mother’s virtue and the hardship she receives.
He read: ﴿وَبِالْوَالِدَيْنِ إِحْسَانًا﴾ [الإسراء: 23].
Aser said: “What if one of the parents is cruel or abusive?”
Salim replied: “Righteousness does not mean enabling injustice or accepting harm without limits. Duties are understood in the light of Sharia, justice, self-preservation and dignity, and some situations require advice from scholars and specialists.
Aser was silent for a long time. Since his father's death, he has begun to remember small situations for which he did not thank him: a cup of water on a sick night, fixing a door, and waiting at school.
He went out into the street and called his mother. He didn't want to ask her anything. He just wanted to hear her voice and say: “How was your day?”

pages.title: When you disagree and do not be unfair
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
One evening, a discussion broke out between two visitors about religion and politics. The voices rose and the words almost turned into insults. Salim intervened and said: “Stop the dialogue if you cannot maintain respect.”
After they left, I asked Maryam: “Does disagreement allow us to be cruel?”
Salim read: ﴿وَلَا يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ شَنَآنُ قَوْمٍ عَلَىٰ أَلَّا تَعْدِلُوا اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَىٰ﴾ [المائدة: 8].
Then he said: “This verse contains a difficult task: Doesn’t hatred make us abandon justice? Justice does not mean that all statements are true, but rather that we rule fairly and preserve rights.”
Daniel said: “In fairness, we may need to admit that we made a mistake in describing those with whom we disagree.”
Aser lowered his head. He remembered a sarcastic comment he had posted one day about believers, which had reduced millions of people to one cruel image. He opened his phone and deleted the comment, not out of fear of anyone, but because he no longer saw sarcasm as evidence of intelligence.
“Sometimes the beginning of the truth is to stop hurting those who don’t look like us,” Maryam said.

pages.title: Chapter on supplication
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
Maryam returned to the library on a day that was not her usual routine. She sat silent until Aser asked her how she was. “My mother is in the hospital, and I don’t know what will happen,” she said.
Salim did not try to promise her a sure recovery. He said: “I ask God to heal her and help you.” In the Islamic perception, supplication is an open door between the servant and his Lord, but the answer to the supplication does not necessarily happen what we asked for in the form and time we want.
It read: ﴿وَإِذَا سَأَلَكَ عِبَادِي عَنِّي فَإِنِّي قَرِيبٌ﴾ [البقرة: 186].
Aser said: “Can a person who is confused in his faith pray?”
Salim said: “He can address God sincerely for guidance, and ask Him for the truth. Supplication does not require fancy language, but rather a sincere heart.”
Maryam said: “I will pray for my mother in my language and what I believe in, and I appreciate your prayers for her.”
When she got up, Aser put his hand on her shoulder. He could not find a phrase that would remove fear, but he knew that having someone next to you on a long night could be a form of mercy.

pages.title: What God sees and people do not see
pages.section: Islam is in the details of life
pages.content:
Daniel asked: “Why is the word intention repeated in our speech? Aren't the apparent actions that matter?
“Actions matter, and intention matters too,” Salim said. A person may give money to help a needy person, and another person may give the same money to buy people’s praise. The appearance is similar, but the intent is different.”
He mentioned the hadith of the Prophet, peace and blessings of God be upon him: “Actions are but by intentions” [Agreed upon], then he said: “This does not mean that good intentions permit a forbidden action or erase a right that we have transgressed.”
Aser said: “So religion is not satisfied with what we tell others about ourselves.”
“That's right,” said Salim. An authentic hadith mentions that God does not look at images and money, but at hearts and deeds [Narrated by Muslim].”
Maryam looked at the street lights and said, “We are tired of a world that demands that we always appear better than we are.”
Aser replied: “Maybe it liberates a person to know that his value is not reduced by his image on the screen.”
That night, he left his phone away from his bed and wrote just three words: “Be honest first.”

pages.title: The message that no one responds to
pages.content:
A month after the first meeting, Aser found an old voice message from his father. He pressed play, and heard a familiar voice saying: “Don’t tire yourself, my son, everything will be easier.” Then the recording ended.
He repeated it a second time and a third time. He knew that the number would not answer him if he called, but his heart had not yet learned the meaning of absence.
In the library, he said in a broken voice: “You told me about the meaning of life.” Now I want to understand death.”
Salim said: “The Qur’an does not present death as a final annihilation for man in the Islamic conception, but rather a transition from this world to another stage followed by resurrection and reckoning. But it does not make sadness over loss a weakness of faith.”
It read: ﴿كُلُّ نَفْسٍ ذَائِقَةُ الْمَوْتِ﴾ [آل عمران: 185].
Maryam said: “The phrase reminds us that death does not distinguish between a believer and a non-believer, rich and poor.”
Daniel said: “As for what comes after it, our religious perceptions differ, and each of us researches and contemplates.”
Aser put the phone back in his pocket. He felt that the first thing a person does in the face of death is to ask for the voice of the one he loves; Perhaps this is why the question about the afterlife does not end at the borders of philosophy.

pages.title: Life between two souls
pages.content:
That morning the sea was unusually calm. The four sat on stone benches and Aser said: “If we are all going to die, why should we labor to build, love, and work?”
Salim replied: “Because the limited time does not cancel its value. On the contrary, it makes choices valuable. In Islam, this world is considered a field for work, and a person is not required to abandon it or spoil it under the pretext that the afterlife remains.
“I may not be able to prevent the end,” said Maryam, “but I can choose how I fill the days before it.”
Daniel said: “Immortality is not a condition for every meaning; It may be a short moment of loyalty that is deeper than years wasted in cruelty.”
Salim said: “The Qur’an teaches us that money and children are a trial and a test, and that deeds are the subject of consideration. Life should not be measured by its length alone.”
Aser stood, drawing a circle in the sand with his foot, then a small wave erased it. In the past, he felt that the disappearance of an impact would make it worthless, but now he wondered: Perhaps life is not measured by what remains of our names, but rather by what we do while we are here, and by what we hope for with God.

pages.title: Beyond the door
pages.content:
Aser said: “Tell me about the isthmus, but do not describe to me things that have not been proven in the text.”
Salim answered: “The isthmus in Islamic belief is a stage between death and resurrection. We believe in what the revelation has told us about the unseen, and we stop at its limits. God Almighty said: ﴿وَمِنْ وَرَائِهِمْ بَرْزَخٌ إِلَىٰ يَوْمِ يُبْعَثُونَ﴾ [المؤمنون: 100]».
“This is different from the knowledge we experience with our senses,” Daniel said. “We have to be clear about what type of claim we are talking about.”
Salim nodded: “Yes. Whoever believes in the revelation accepts its information from the unseen, but whoever does not yet believe may first ask about the truthfulness of the source of the information.”
Maryam said: “In times of loss, we miss details, so we fill the silence with perceptions whose veracity we do not know.”
Aser said: “I want to respect the unknown instead of making up comforting stories for it.”
The answer did not reveal to him the world after death, but it taught him a rare difference: saying “I believe in what was stated” is not the same as claiming that you saw with your own eyes what is beyond absence.

pages.title: The day the business unfolds
pages.content:
Daniel was carrying a book about perceptions of the Day of Judgment in the Abrahamic religions. He said: “Justice among believers is linked to the idea that the oppressor may escape the punishment of this world, but he does not escape the justice of God.”
Salim said: “In Islam, Muslims believe in resurrection, reckoning, and reward, and that God does not wrong anyone. The Qur’an says: ﴿فَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَيْرًا يَرَهُ ۝ وَمَنْ يَعْمَلْ مِثْقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ شَرًّا يَرَهُ﴾ [الزلزلة: 7–8]».
Aser asked: “Are small things counted too?”
"Yes. This deepens the meaning of responsibility. But it does not cancel out the mercy and forgiveness mentioned in the texts.”
Maryam said: “I think about those who lived and died without anyone hearing their stories, or getting justice.”
Daniel said: “The idea of ​​justice that goes beyond the limits of the world is profound, even as we differ in understanding its details.”
Aser remembers a worker who was wronged by a company and then closed his file unfairly. For the first time he thought of Judgment Day not simply as a personal fear, but as a question about rights that might be lost to the records of the earth but not lost, in faith, to God.

pages.title: Between fear and hope
pages.content:
Aser asked: “Why are there so many images of heaven and hell in religious texts? Isn't it enough to talk about love?
Salim said: “The Qur’an combines promise and threat, hope and fear, and describes God’s mercy and justice. Moral life is not a pleasant feeling alone; “It contains real responsibility for the evil we do, and real hope for forgiveness.”
Then he read: ﴿نَبِّئْ عِبَادِي أَنِّي أَنَا الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ ۝ وَأَنَّ عَذَابِي هُوَ الْعَذَابُ الْأَلِيمُ﴾ [الحجر: 49–50].
Maryam said: “It is wrong for religion to turn into a constant threat that erases mercy, just as it is wrong for mercy to turn into a denial of accountability.”
Daniel said: “We must not judge the final fate of certain people without knowledge. “These are more subtle matters than our emotions.”
“Yes,” Salim replied. God knows best about creation, what has reached them, their structures and conditions, and His final judgment.”
Aser looked at his hands. He wished the world to be both just and merciful; Perhaps one of the most difficult questions is how the two matters come together without injustice or tolerance of injustice.

pages.title: Do not despair of mercy
pages.content:
The next night Aser confessed to something he had been hiding. “I'm not proud of everything I've done,” he said. I hurt people, betrayed a friend's trust, and walked away from my mother when she needed me. "I'm afraid it will be too late to come back."
Salim said: “As long as you live, do not let regret be a reason for despair. God says: ﴿قُلْ يَا عِبَادِيَ الَّذِينَ أَسْرَفُوا عَلَىٰ أَنْفُسِهِمْ لَا تَقْنَطُوا مِنْ رَحْمَةِ اللَّهِ﴾ [الزمر: 53]».
Aser asked: “Is ‘sorry’ enough?”
He said: “Sincere repentance is not just a word; It involves abandoning sin and remorse, resolving not to return, restoring rights to their rightful owners, or asking for forgiveness when a human right is involved, depending on the case.”
Maryam said: “Coming back is courageous, but it does not erase the impact of what we did to others in one moment.”
Aser took out his phone and wrote his old friend a short message: “I did you wrong. I don't ask for you to forget, but I want to confess and make amends as much as I can. He looked at it for a long time, then sent it. He didn't know if he would get a response, but he knew that he was finally beginning to accept his responsibility.

pages.title: Don't force the sun to rise
pages.content:
“We are no longer four strangers,” said Daniel. But we still differ in faith. Does this result disappoint you, Salim?
The man laughed quietly: “If our relationship turns into a race to gather supporters, I will have ruined the meaning of dialogue.” “I believe in my message and I explain it, but guidance is not something I do through pressure.”
It read: ﴿إِنَّكَ لَا تَهْدِي مَنْ أَحْبَبْتَ وَلَٰكِنَّ اللَّهَ يَهْدِي مَنْ يَشَاءُ﴾ [القصص: 56].
“I am still a Christian, and I understand Islam more clearly,” Maryam said. I do not want anyone to pretend that our dispute is over, nor to turn it into animosity.”
Daniel said: “And I will return to my texts and questions with what I learned from this dialogue.”
Aser looked at them. He had thought that the religious debate would only end with the victory of one party and the defeat of the other. But now they were in front of him: three researchers and a man who shared his belief, and no one pulled the chair from under the one who disagreed. He felt that kindness did not validate a doctrine, but it might make the search for truth more equitable.

pages.title: The message that arrived
pages.content:
Aser's phone rang as he stood in front of the library. It was a message from his old friend: “I appreciate your apology. "I'm really hurt, and I need time, but I'm glad you confessed."
Aser sat on the stone steps and read it twice. He didn't get complete forgiveness, nor an easy ending, but he felt like a door had opened.
Salim came out and asked him: “What’s wrong with you?”
He said: “I thought what I needed most was an answer about death.” “I discovered that I also needed a way to live before death.”
“This is one of the most important questions,” Salim said. Faith that does not affect honesty, trustworthiness, and mercy remains far from achieving its desired effect.”
Aser asked: “Can I read the entire Qur’an slowly, with explanation, and ask when I don’t understand?”
He replied: “This is the best place to start with.” Read with an open heart and an attentive mind. And do not be afraid to say, “I don’t know.”
Aser raised his eyes to the sky. The clouds were dispersing, but the whole world had not changed. But he no longer wanted to run away from her or his questions.

pages.title: Praying at the window
pages.content:
On the last night of their usual meetings, Aser sat alone in front of the window of his room; The same window that witnessed the first question after his father's death. The old picture was in place, and the rain was on the glass, but his heart was no longer what it was.
He opened the Qur’an at Surat Al-Fatihah, read the translation of the meanings and interpretation, then re-heard the verses in Arabic. Stop when God Almighty says: ﴿اهْدِنَا الصِّرَاطَ الْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ [الفاتحة: 6].
He was not ready to declare a certainty that was not complete in himself. But he realized that he could be sincere in seeking the truth. He placed his hands in front of him and said in a low voice: “O Lord, if you are the truth that my heart is searching for, lead me to you.” I mean to follow the truth wherever it is, not where I would like it to be.”
He saw no miracle in the room. The sky did not suddenly brighten. The rain stayed raining, and it was one hour. But something important happened: for the first time, the question was not a wall between him and the world, but a path on which he could walk without lying to himself.

pages.title: When man asked: Who created me?
pages.content:
In the morning, Aser opened the door of “Dar Al-Sual” and found him groaning as usual. Maryam was reading at the window, Daniel was writing notes in the margins of his book, and Salim was watering a small plant near the door.
Aser said: “I came months ago to find one sentence that would end my confusion. Now I have more questions, but I am not afraid of them as much as I used to.”
“Because seeking the truth is not a show of certainty,” Salim said. Whoever believes continues to learn, whoever searches continues to question, and everyone must strive for honesty and justice.”
Maryam smiled: “And not to reduce the other to his name or religion.”
Daniel added: “And not to close the book at the first statement that contradicts what we know.”
Aser opened his notebook to the first page, where he wrote one day: “Where do people go when they die?” Underneath it is now written: “What will I do with the days I have left?”
At the bottom of the page he placed the verse that accompanies it: ﴿سَنُرِيهِمْ آيَاتِنَا فِي الْآفَاقِ وَفِي أَنْفُسِهِمْ﴾ [فصلت: 53].
Close the notebook quietly. The end of the story was not for the reader to be forced to make a decision, but for a window to be opened for him. Whoever knows that he does not have an endless life may realize that the greatest questions do not deserve ridicule or escape, but rather deserve an honest heart searching for God, meaning, and goodness.
Here the pages of the novel end, but the question does not end.
